title: Attribute "optimize" not supported by some clang compilers and causes warning
body:
Here:
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/blob/8f922cdc7cc6de2344e75ddd657889f4ff761790/Include/system_stm32h7xx.h#L88

Description of the problem: [see in the forum](https://community.st.com/t5/stm32cubeide-for-visual-studio/warning-quot-unknown-attribute-optimize-quot-stm32cubeide-vscode/td-p/884776)

Proposed change: add check for attribute "optimize" in the #if line above:

```
#if defined(__GNUC__) && __has_attribute(optimize)
```

More to this.... My AI assistant says...

>    placing __attribute__(optimize) only on the function prototype in a header is not guaranteed to work.
>   For reliable behavior, you should place the attribute on the function definition in the C file, not just the declaration.
>   **Why the attribute must be on the definition**
>   GCC applies optimization attributes at the point where the function is compiled, which is the definition, not the declaration.
>   If the definition lacks the attribute  ..... Then GCC will simply ignore the attribute from the prototype
> 

If this is correct, the #if/#else with attribute "optimize" should be undone (reverted to ver. 1.10.5) in the .h file and the attribute inserted in all variants of `system_stm32h7xx****.c` on the body of function  `ExitRun0Mode`

title: Incorrect values in D1CorePrescTable
body: **Describe the set-up** Stm32H7xx **Describe the bug** The `D1CorePrescTable` is incorrectly initialized to `{0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9}` and used for both 3-bit and 4-bit prescalers. This issue has been raised several times in different places. However, due to some brain malfunction, the previous issue reported in this repository was closed with the following explanation (#12): > The current D1CorePrescTable[16] is implemented to support both 4-bits dividers like D1CPRE and 3-bits dividers such as D1PPRE, D2PPRE2, D2PPRE1. The thing is - you **CANNOT** implement this table to support both types of prescalers. **How To Reproduce** Open code base, search for `D1CorePrescTable`. **Additional context** The simplest solution would be to use two separate tables. To explain it further - one table for 3-bit prescalers and one table for 4-bit prescalers. So there is **two** tables in the end. No, you cannot keep single table for both prescalers, I'm sorry. **Other issues describing the problem** https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/issues/12 https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeH7/issues/301 **Screenshots** Relevant examples describing the 3-bit and 4-bit prescalers values from the reference manual for STMH7xx - in case anyone developing the ST libraries has problem to read the documentation:

comments.author: ALABSTM
comments.body:
Hi @radoslav06,

I hope you are doing fine. I agree this point is more than tricky, especially if one focuses on the table itself, instead of tracking the **whole trail** from application to drivers.

However, once clarified, you will see how all pieces **fit together** and how the whole stuff works **perfectly fine** both for 4-bit and 3-bit prescalers.

> [!TIP]
> Two points to keep in mind:
> 1. The `D1CorePrescTable[]` table returns the necessary **number of right shifts** in order to achieve the desired clock frequency **division**.
> 2. Only a **set of predefined** values are **allowed** as indices of the `D1CorePrescTable[]` table.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For point 2 above to be enforced, it is necessary that the application uses that **set of predefined** values, not arbitrary ones.

----

Let's dive into the details of an existing example, the [RCC Clock Configuration](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeH7/tree/master/Projects/NUCLEO-H745ZI-Q/Examples/RCC/RCC_ClockConfig) for instance:

* The `D1CorePrescTable[]` table is defined in the [system_stm32h7xx.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeH7/blob/f5c0b7a2b1f6eb26fde150f72edb2d7deb647066/Projects/NUCLEO-H745ZI-Q/Examples/RCC/RCC_ClockConfig/Common/Src/system_stm32h7xx.c#L111) **CMSIS** file as follows:

```c
  const  uint8_t D1CorePrescTable[16] = {0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9};
```

* At application level, the values to set the **4-bit** fields `HPRE` and `D1CPRE` of register `RCC_D1CFGR`, and the **3-bit** fields `D2PPRE1` and `D2PPRE2` of register `RCC_D2CFGR` are selected from a **predefined set** of values, in `SystemClock_Config()` from the [main.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeH7/blob/e109a24f043ec5e6d446c7a8ef31aa57029c7168/Projects/NUCLEO-H745ZI-Q/Examples/RCC/RCC_ClockConfig/CM7/Src/main.c#L215-L222) file, as shown below:

```c
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.SYSCLKDivider  = RCC_SYSCLK_DIV1; /* D1CPRE  */
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.AHBCLKDivider  = RCC_HCLK_DIV2;   /* HPRE    */
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.APB1CLKDivider = RCC_APB1_DIV2;   /* D2PPRE1 */
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.APB2CLKDivider = RCC_APB2_DIV2;   /* D2PPRE2 */
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.APB3CLKDivider = RCC_APB3_DIV2;   /* D1PPRE  */
  RCC_ClkInitStruct.APB4CLKDivider = RCC_APB4_DIV2;   /* D3PPRE  */
```

----

* Let's start with the **4-bit** field `D1CPRE`. The predefined values `RCC_SYSCLK_DIVx` are found in the [stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.h](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/57ed86b4c358e2333a71fd895b17f1ccdb68739e/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.h#L350-L358) **HAL** file. They are **aliases** of definitions found in the [stm32h745xx.h](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/blob/v1.10.6/Include/stm32h745xx.h) **CMSIS** header file.

```c
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV1                RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV1   /* 0x000 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV2                RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV2   /* 0x800 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV4                RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV4   /* 0x900 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV8                RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV8   /* 0xA00 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV16               RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV16  /* 0xB00 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV64               RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV64  /* 0xC00 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV128              RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV128 /* 0xD00 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV256              RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV256 /* 0xE00 */
#define RCC_SYSCLK_DIV512              RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_DIV512 /* 0xF00 */
```
 
* Back to the [system_stm32h7xx.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeH7/blob/f5c0b7a2b1f6eb26fde150f72edb2d7deb647066/Projects/NUCLEO-H745ZI-Q/Examples/RCC/RCC_ClockConfig/Common/Src/system_stm32h7xx.c#L338-L342) **CMSIS** file, we have these two lines in `SystemCoreClockUpdate()`:

```c
  /* Compute SystemClock frequency --------------------------------------------------*/
  tmp = D1CorePrescTable[(RCC->D1CFGR & RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE) >> RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_Pos];

  /* common_system_clock frequency : CM7 CPU frequency  */
  common_system_clock >>= tmp;
```

* Here's how the magic happens:
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_SYSCLK_DIV1` (**i.e.**, `0x000`):
        * Field `D1CPRE` of register `RCC_D1CFGR` would be set to `0x0`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D1CFGR & RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE) >> RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_Pos` would also give **0**,
        * Variable `tmp` would be equal to **0**, the element **0** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` being equal to **0**.
        * Then, there would be **no shift** at line `common_system_clock >>= tmp;`, meaning **no frequency division**.
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_SYSCLK_DIV2` (**i.e.**, `0x800`):
        * Field `D1CPRE` of register `RCC_D1CFGR` would be set to `0x8`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D1CFGR & RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE) >> RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_Pos` would give **8** this time (`RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_Pos` being defined in the **CMSIS** header file and equal to `8`),
        * Variable `tmp` would be equal to **1**, the element **8** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` being equal to **1**.
        * Then, there would be **one shift** at line `common_system_clock >>= tmp;`, corresponding to a frequency division **by 2**.
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_SYSCLK_DIV512` (**i.e.**, `0xF00`):
        * Field `D1CPRE` of register `RCC_D1CFGR` would be set to `0xF`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D1CFGR & RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE) >> RCC_D1CFGR_D1CPRE_Pos` would give **15** this time,
        * Variable `tmp` would be equal to **9**, the element **15** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` being equal to **9**.
        * Then, there would be **nine shifts** at line `common_system_clock >>= tmp;`, corresponding to a frequency division **by 512**.
    * And so on... You can check with the rest of predefined values.

> [!NOTE]
> The same applies to the other **4-bit** field `HPRE` and the predefined values `RCC_HCLK_DIVx`.

----

* Let's continue with the **3-bit** field `D2PPRE1`. The predefined values `RCC_APB1_DIVx` are found in the [stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.h](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/57ed86b4c358e2333a71fd895b17f1ccdb68739e/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.h#L427-L431) **HAL** file. They too are **aliases** of definitions found in the [stm32h745xx.h](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/blob/v1.10.6/Include/stm32h745xx.h) **CMSIS** header file.

```c
#define RCC_APB1_DIV1                  RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_DIV1  /* 0x00 */
#define RCC_APB1_DIV2                  RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_DIV2  /* 0x40 */
#define RCC_APB1_DIV4                  RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_DIV4  /* 0x50 */
#define RCC_APB1_DIV8                  RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_DIV8  /* 0x60 */
#define RCC_APB1_DIV16                 RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_DIV16 /* 0x70 */
```
 
* In the [stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/57ed86b4c358e2333a71fd895b17f1ccdb68739e/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.c#L1521) **HAL** file, we have this line in `HAL_RCC_GetPCLK1Freq()`:

```c
  return (HAL_RCC_GetHCLKFreq() >> ((D1CorePrescTable[(RCC->D2CFGR & RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1) >> RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_Pos]) & 0x1FU));
```

* Following the same reasoning:
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_APB1_DIV1` (**i.e.**, `0x00`):
        * Field `D2PPRE1` of register `RCC_D2CFGR` would be set to `0x0`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D2CFGR & RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1) >> RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_Pos` would also give **0**,
        * Since element **0** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` is equal to **0**, there would be **no shift**, meaning **no frequency division**.
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_APB1_DIV2` (**i.e.**, `0x40`):
        * Field `D2PPRE1` of register `RCC_D2CFGR` would be set to `0x4`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D2CFGR & RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1) >> RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_Pos` would give **4** this time (`RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_Pos` being defined in the **CMSIS** header file and equal to `4`),
        * Since element **4** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` is equal to **1**, there would be **one shift**, corresponding to a frequency division **by 2**.
    * If, at **application** level, the selected value is `RCC_APB1_DIV16` (**i.e.**, `0x70`):
        * Field `D2PPRE1` of register `RCC_D2CFGR` would be set to `0x7`,
        * The index evaluation `(RCC->D2CFGR & RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1) >> RCC_D2CFGR_D2PPRE1_Pos` would give **7** this time,
        * Since element **7** of `D1CorePrescTable[]` is equal to **4**, there would be **four shifts**, corresponding to a frequency division **by 16**.
    * And so on...

> [!NOTE]
> The same applies to the other **3-bit** fields like `D2PPRE2` and the predefined values `RCC_APB2_DIVx`, for instance.

----

### Conclusion

To understand how all pieces **fit together** and how the whole stuff works **perfectly fine** both for 4-bit and 3-bit prescalers, one has to look at the **whole trail** from application to drivers, not just focus on the table itself.

As you can see, both **4-bit** and **3-bit** prescalers are **cleverly** handled using a **single** table `D1CorePrescTable[]`.
* Elements **0** and **8 to 15** correspond to the **4-bit** prescalers,
* Elements **0** and **4 to 7** correspond to the **3-bit** prescalers,
* Elements **1 to 3** are just **placeholders** to make everything perfectly fit together,

----

I hope this clarifies the point. Please allow me to close this issue.

With regards,

comments.author: radoslav06
comments.body:
Hi @ALABSTM,

There is no "perfect fit" in this solution, let me explain it in a different way and let's touch different points here:

1. Wrong values
Let's clarify one thing at the beginning - the table contains wrong values according to the reference manual as there are conflicts between both prescalers, namely on values between 4-7:

Bit Pattern | Register Value | 4-bit divider | 3-bit divider | Current Table Value
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
0100 | 4 | Divide by 1 (Shift 0) | Divide by 2 (Shift 1) | Shift 1
0101 | 5 | Divide by 1 (Shift 0) | Divide by 4 (Shift 2) | Shift 2
0110 | 6 | Divide by 1 (Shift 0) | Divide by 8 (Shift 3) | Shift 3
0111 | 7 | Divide by 1 (Shift 0) | Divide by 16 (Shift 4) | Shift 4

**This is clearly wrong.** I cannot explain it better.

2. Wrong assumptions
Your description assumes that the clocks were setup with your code that takes into account the incorrect table values and they were never changed.  The expected behavior (at least in my opinion) is that the function calculates the correct clocks' values based on hardware register values (all possible values). This is the correct approach taking into account best practices, covering 100% hardware behavior, defense programming techniques and physical hardware effects like bit-flips.

3. Bad design
It is a *very* bad practice to ignore an error in one place and try to mask it in another place in a system. I don't even know how to comment that kind of approach. Errors shall be fixed at the place of occurrence.

4. Public interface
The mentioned table is not an internal design only. The table is exposed with `extern` declaration in the header file, so it shall be considered as a public interface. So you are exposing public interfaces that is simply wrong.

To be honest I am quite astonished that this was reported to you several times and every time you defend your incorrect implementation and refuse to fix that. That says a lot about your quality standards.

I see that you close the issue, I disagree with that, but that's your decision; I am not here to teach. I just voluntarily reported an error, giving you the extensive description, so you have a chance to improve your software. It seems for me that I wasted my time here and it is not worth to report any bugs to you.

Taking into account all the above, the case is closed also for me.

Best regards,
R

title: Document suggestion: Change the encoding of the ld file to UTF-8.
body:
In this repository, all ".ld" files have minor differences in their comments compared to other repositories. The quotes around "as is," are encoded in Windows-1252, whereas other repositories do not have these quotes. It's recommended to remove them.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/blob/74b62d0bfa82e082c0610ff6a9137805df3cd192/Source/Templates/gcc/linker/stm32h745xg_flash_CM4.ld#L17-L19

With Regards,

comments.author: demopath
comments.body: The symbols in the comments were actually minor issues and didn't affect program compilation at all. However, I ran into trouble when using Python to remove those comments for preprocessing simplification (this problem was easily handled and has already been solved). The issue was that this symbol caused the entire file's encoding to be recognized as Windows-1252, leading to problems when trying to process it with UTF-8. That's why I mentioned it.

title: Incorrect `GPIO_MODER_MODE[10:15]_{Pos,Msk}` definitions
body:
While reviewing #20, I noticed that some of the now-legacy `GPIO_MODER_MODExx` defines are incorrect. The last column got cut off for those with a two digit number.  In 6 places, `Po` and `Ms` should be `Pos` and `Msk`. This appears to apply to all H7 parts.

```

#define GPIO_MODER_MODE9_Msk           GPIO_MODER_MODER9_Msk
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE9               GPIO_MODER_MODER9
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE9_0             GPIO_MODER_MODER9_0
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE9_1             GPIO_MODER_MODER9_1

#define GPIO_MODER_MODE10_Pos          GPIO_MODER_MODER10_Po
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE10_Msk          GPIO_MODER_MODER10_Ms
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE10              GPIO_MODER_MODER10
#define GPIO_MODER_MODE10_0            GPIO_MODER_MODER10_0
```

title: Is it planned to remove old code and macros?
body:
CMSIS device files (headers) are very large, and changes are periodically made like: https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis-device-h7/commit/e4d57d6edc39f35aced298732829fc2a5e6a8a71

This brings each time a section with `Legacy xxx`
This is almost doubling the code, old + new.

Is it planned to remove the old code or is it left for compatibility and will never be removed?.
If for compatibility, then if it is with us forever, why introduce new names for the same thing if the old code will 100% not be removed?

If at least some plans for a large-scale refactoring that will remove old definitions?

I ask because I would like to have synchronized versions of these files with the official repository.

But if this refactoring is not planned, we will plan refactoring in our repository, because old/new code with a many of developers leads to an increase in entropy.

Thank you.

comments.author: ALABSTM
comments.body:
Hi @KoynovStas,

Could you please clarify more what is meant by "an increase in entropy"?

Thank you,

comments.author: KoynovStas
comments.body:
Sorry for my bad English. I meant that some our developers use the old version, others the new one. This leads to the fact that some code uses old defines, others new ones. 
If you do not have plans to remove the old code, our Tech Leads would have removed the old code in our repositories. Yes, we will have to update our copy manually when releasing new versions.
But this will force everyone to write driver code with one version of definitions.

comments.author: ASEHSTM
comments.body:
Hello @KoynovStas,

The legacy code is maintained for compatibility reasons and will not be removed. 
Developers have the discretion to choose which version to use. However, we strongly recommend utilizing the new code for any new development.

Thank you.
With Regards,

comments.author: KoynovStas
comments.body: Thank you for the official response.

title: Incorrect ETH_DMADSR_RPS Register Definitions
body:
**Describe the set-up**
STM32H743

**Describe the bug**
For STM32H743 (and probably all other h7 and h5 which have ethernet) the [defines](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_h7/blob/13ba9da797a30e1563a8795f974425fb26dd0457/Include/stm32h743xx.h#L8370) for `ETH_DMADSR_RPS_X_POS` are shifted by 4 (and `ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING` has wrong comment).

```c
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_Pos                            (8U)
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_Msk                            (0xFUL << ETH_DMADSR_RPS_Pos) /*!< 0x00000F00 */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS                                ETH_DMADSR_RPS_Msk       /* DMA Channel Receive Process State */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_STOPPED                        (0U)   /* Stopped (Reset or Stop Receive Command issued) */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_FETCHING_Pos                   (12U)
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_FETCHING_Msk                   (0x1UL << ETH_DMADSR_RPS_FETCHING_Pos) /*!< 0x00001000 */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_FETCHING                       ETH_DMADSR_RPS_FETCHING_Msk /* Running (Fetching Rx Transfer Descriptor) */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING_Pos                    (12U)
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING_Msk                    (0x3UL << ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING_Pos) /*!< 0x00003000 */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING                        ETH_DMADSR_RPS_WAITING_Msk /* Running (Waiting for status) */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_SUSPENDED_Pos                  (14U)
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_SUSPENDED_Msk                  (0x1UL << ETH_DMADSR_RPS_SUSPENDED_Pos) /*!< 0x00004000 */
#define ETH_DMADSR_RPS_SUSPENDED                      ETH_DMADSR_RPS_SUSPENDED_Msk /* Suspended (Rx Descriptor Unavailable) */
```

title: Pseudo-random behavior of GCC start-up template when main() returns
body:
Board: NUCLEO-H723ZG
Compiler: arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arch Repository) 14.1.0

The GCC start-up assembly template for the H723xx [(see here)](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_h7/blob/13ba9da797a30e1563a8795f974425fb26dd0457/Source/Templates/gcc/startup_stm32h723xx.s) contains the following code at the end of `Reset_Handler`:

```
/* Call static constructors */
  bl __libc_init_array
/* Call the application's entry point.*/
  bl  main
  bx  lr
```

Usually, `main` is assumed not to return. However, if it does, the next instruction `BX LR` will jump to the address stored in the link register. This address will usually be the return address for the last sub-routine call inside `main`. So, this instruction will jump back into `main` to a more or less random location. In my particular case, this location was close to the end of `main`, and execution continued through to the end of `main` where it pop-ed a value of zero into the program counter. This then triggered a hard fault, because zero is not a thumb mode address, and the default hard fault handler (an infinite loop) was entered.

Of course, one can debate about the desired behavior if `main` returns, but I think we can agree the current behavior is not it. One approach would be to replace `BX LR` with an infinite loop, similar to the GCC start-up templates for the H5 series. See for example this snippet below (taken from [here](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_h5/blob/9a778e0f162bd21200647adafb922d50b2c60f81/Source/Templates/gcc/startup_stm32h563xx.s)):

```
/* Call static constructors */
  bl __libc_init_array
/* Call the application's entry point.*/
  bl main

LoopForever:
    b LoopForever
```

One could also consider throwing in a call to `__libc_fini_array()` after `main` and before the infinite loop for symmetry.

comments.author: sidneycadot
comments.body:
I had a cursory look at some different stm32 mcu's startup code assembly, it appears that this is done this way across the startup code of more STM32 families; the nonsensical "bx lr" and the missing __libc_fini_array() call is also in the F4 startup code. The H5 startup code has an infinite loop after return from main() -- but no call to _libc_fini_array().

It would be best to homogenize this across all families, I think. That would take a sweep across a bunch of repositories.

In general, the behavior when returning from main() should be documented. If the choice is made to not touch the current implementation (for fear of breaking stuff, for example), I'd like to see a clear statement somewhere in the documentation that returning from main() triggers undefined behavior. I wouldn't favor that approach, but it's better than having UB and *not* documenting it.

Hi Rania,
I think you are confusing the bit number with the bit mask:
`(0x3UL << FMC_SDCMR_MODE_Pos)` means `0b0011` which is definitely not MODE[2] bit.
`(0x4UL << FMC_SDCMR_MODE_Pos)` means `0b0100`.

```
#define FMC_SDCMR_MODE_1           (0x2UL << FMC_SDCMR_MODE_Pos)                /*!< 0x00000002 */
#define FMC_SDCMR_MODE_2           (0x4UL << FMC_SDCMR_MODE_Pos)                /*!< 0x00000004 */
```

title: Reset_Handler resets variables set by SystemInit()
body:
The very detailed report was done for https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_l4/issues/2
This issue is not present on some lines, e.g. F4. And present on the majority of others, like L4, G0, H7, etc.
Please fix the order of initialisation - data/bss section first, then SystemInit(), second.

comments.author: TOUNSTM
comments.body:
Hello @cpq,

As mentioned in the previous issue https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_l4/issues/2, the main reason for this change is the use of external memories. When using external memory, it is crucial to initialize the memory controller before accessing any variables stored in that memory. This is why SystemInit() must be called before initializing the data and BSS sections.

In the SystemInit() API, there are no variables like SystemCoreClock; instead, it directly accesses hardware registers to configure the system. We have thoroughly tested this approach and have not encountered any cases where SystemCoreClock is equal to 0.
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_h7/blob/13ba9da797a30e1563a8795f974425fb26dd0457/Source/Templates/system_stm32h7xx.c#L175-L301
By calling SystemInit() first, we ensure that the external memory is properly configured, allowing the subsequent initialization of the data and BSS sections to proceed without issues.

I hope this clarifies the rationale behind the change. Thank you for your understanding. Allow me to close this issue.

Kind regards,

comments.author: cpq
comments.body:
@TOUNSTM 

I don't know what do you mean by `In the SystemInit() API, there are no variables like SystemCoreClock`.
Maybe if you take a look at the CMSIS documentation, https://www.keil.com/pack/doc/CMSIS_Dev/Core/html/group__system__init__gr.html , you'll find that `uint32_t SystemCoreClock` is there, and must be defined by the device code.

Unless you're implementing some other CMSIS, not ARM.

Nevertheless, as I pointed out elsewhere, some of the ST device CMSIS startup code call SystemInit() before data/BSS init. Some - after.  So your argument "This is why SystemInit() must be called before initializing the data and BSS sections" may be valid, but it contradicts your own practice. Like here, for F4 series:
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_f4/blob/73273c20e85c6c57688f6106485a2e4f2592ddf9/Source/Templates/gcc/startup_stm32f429xx.s#L95-L99

So please don't fill me bullshit. If you don't want to fix thing, just admit it - there could be valid reason, like  legacy, breaking existing code, etc etc.  Adding an "invalid" label does not make the issue invalid, maybe in your own mind only.

comments.author: TOUNSTM
comments.body:
Hello @cpq,

We understand your concerns and appreciate your feedback. The initialization of the data and BSS sections before calling SystemInit() is indeed a common practice in embedded systems development. However, in certain scenarios, particularly when using external memory, it is necessary to call SystemInit() before initializing the data and BSS sections to ensure proper memory configuration.
> Nevertheless, as I pointed out elsewhere, some of the ST device CMSIS startup code call SystemInit() before data/BSS init. Some - after. So your argument "This is why SystemInit() must be called before initializing the data and BSS sections" may be valid, but it contradicts your own practice. Like here, for F4 series: https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_f4/blob/73273c20e85c6c57688f6106485a2e4f2592ddf9/Source/Templates/gcc/startup_stm32f429xx.s#L95-L99

In our specific case, this approach is essential to ensure the correct operation of the system. You can refer to a recent version of the F4 series, where you will see that the issue has been addressed in the same manner.
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/cmsis_device_f4/blob/cdbad761857acedcdd07ece7939b4cb209ed826a/Source/Templates/gcc/startup_stm32f429xx.s#L63-L100

While your perspective is valid in general terms, it is not applicable to our specific situation due to the need for external memory initialization. We hope this clarifies our approach and the rationale behind it.

Thank you for your understanding.

The headers also seem to be missing a few definitions (`__VTOR_PRESENT`, `__FPU_DP`, and `__DTCM_PRESENT`) that are present in the template from the included version of CMSIS.

title: Allow VECT_TAB_OFFSET to be set externally
body:
Currently, in order to change the value of VECT_TAB_OFFSET, the user has to modify the `system_stm32h7xx.c` file. This is inconvenient in cases where the value has to change for different builds.

If the code was changed from:

```c
#define VECT_TAB_OFFSET         0x00000000U
```

to 

```c
#ifndef VECT_TAB_OFFSET
#define VECT_TAB_OFFSET         0x00000000U
#endif
```

The user could define the value via a command line, like so `-DVECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x00020000`.

please check **PM0253** _STM32F7 Series and STM32H7 Series Cortex®-M7 processor programming manual_ (Rev 5)

**4.3.4 Vector table offset register**
The table alignment requirements mean that **bits [8:0]** of the table offset are always **zero**.

`0x300 -> 001100000000b`

comments.author: ALABSTM
comments.body:
Hi @carlo-dev-git,

I sent your question back to our development teams and they confirm your doubts. Actually, the VTO should be a multiple of `0x400` for both single- and dual-core part-numbers.

We do apologize for this inconvenience. I will reopen this issue pending the fix publication.

With regards,

title: stm32h743xx.h: wrong definition of FLASH_CRCCR_ALL_BANK_Pos
body:
The **FLASH_CRCCR_ALL_BANK_Pos** definition is set to 22.
According to the RM0433 Rev 7 (February 2020), the ALL_BANK bit in FLASH_CRCCR1 is bit 7.
The correct value for FLASH_CRCCR_ALL_BANK_Pos should be:

`#define FLASH_CRCCR_ALL_BANK_Pos             (7U)`

comments.author: ASELSTM
comments.body:
Hi @deadror ,

Thank you for your contribution.

We raised this issue to our development teams, and they confirmed that the ALL_BANK bit is defined at bit 22 instead of bit 7. 

Indeed, the ALL_BANK bit in CUT1.0 has indeed been defined at bit 7, and it has been moved to bit 22 in the new CUT2.0. So, the problem is rather related to the documentation. 

In fact, this version of the reference manual is not yet updated with the new position of the ALL_BANK bit in the CUT2.0 of the STM32H7 which is bit 22. However, this is in progress. The RM0433 is being updated, the ALL_BANK bit position will be fixed and the new version of the reference manual will be available at a later date.

Since that the issue is not related to the CMSIS device, allow me to close this issue, thank you for your comprehension.

With regards,
